 FaceStealer Cryptocurrency Theft Scheme
 North Korean cyber actors aggressively target companies and individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 industries with highly tailored, hard-to-detect social engineering campaigns, stealing billions of dollars in cryptocurrency in recent years.
 These actors leverage a variety of tactics to compromise targets, including FaceStealer, a highly effective social engineering scheme that uses imposter versions of popular video conferencing platforms, secretly recorded web cam video, and computer intrusions. The FBI attributes this activity to the North Korean hacking group commonly referred to in the private sector as Sapphire Sleet, UNC1069, Stardust Chollima, APT38, and BlueNoroff.
 These actors are increasingly targeting open-source software developers and maintainers using the FaceStealer technique to gain access to their devices and software repository accounts. Their objective is compromise of the software supply chain. By infiltrating accounts of trusted developers and maintainers, the threat actors can potentially distribute malicious code through widely used software, impacting millions of downstream users.
 In November 2026, the FBI and DOJ announced the disruption of cloud-based infrastructure used by North Korean hackers in this scheme. The FBI identified and seized over 900 webcam videos of victims working in the crypto and Web3 industries around the world. Leading up to the disruption, the scheme had resulted in the theft of more than $400 million dollars in the last 18 months.
 The exploit lifecycle 
 1. Threat actors compromise and secretly record victim’s webcam.
 2. Threat actors hijack victim’s communication accounts and message victim’s contacts.
 3. Threat actors deliver convincing fake video link to new target.
 4. Threat actors lure targets into realistic imposter video chats.
 5. Threat actors impersonate original victim with recorded webcam video and trick target to self-infect.
 For more information on the scheme—and best practices to protect yourself from future targeting—read the FBI’s FLASH .
